entities.summary:
Wu Qi (died 380 BCE) was a pivotal figure in ancient Chinese history, a military general, philosopher, and statesman whose career spanned the tumultuous early Warring States period. Serving successively the states of Lu, Wei, and Chu, his radical military and administrative reforms profoundly reshaped the political and strategic landscape of the era. He is celebrated as one of China's most formidable strategists, alongside Sun Tzu, whose work, *Wu Zi*, remains a foundational text in military theory, influencing commanders for over two millennia. His ruthless effectiveness and unwavering commitment to state power epitomized the Legalist ideology gaining prominence during this period of intense competition.

Wu Qi's contributions were manifold and transformative. In the state of Wei, he commanded armies that decisively defeated the powerful Qin state, expanding Wei's territory and establishing it as a dominant military force. His innovative approach to warfare emphasized rigorous training, strict discipline, and meritocratic promotion, transforming peasant conscripts into formidable fighting units. Later, as Chancellor of Chu, he initiated sweeping reforms aimed at centralizing state power: he curtailed the privileges of the Chu aristocracy, abolished hereditary offices, relocated inactive nobles to frontier regions, and reduced official salaries to fund the military. These measures, while temporarily invigorating Chu, earned him the bitter enmity of the entrenched elite.
